summary.oneLiner: Swaraj Engines Ltd is a single-customer diesel-engine maker supplying 20 HP to 65 HP engines exclusively to Mahindra & Mahindra for fitment into 'Swaraj' brand tractors, having cumulatively supplied 1.96 million engines since 1989-90.
summary.business: Swaraj Engines Limited ('SEL') primarily manufactures diesel engines in the 20 HP to 65 HP range for fitment into 'Swaraj' tractors manufactured by Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. ('M&M'), which is also its holding company. Its entire sale is to M&M, with no exports, and it additionally sells engine spares/parts. Operations are run through a lean organisation structure with continuous improvement in process efficiencies and optimised resource utilisation, supported by an SAP ERP system.

Engines: Diesel engines for tractors, 20 HP to 65 HP range (for 'Swaraj' brand tractors)

endMarkets: Indian domestic tractor industry (sole customer M&M - Swaraj division); demand driven by monsoon, crop realisations, government interventions and pace of farm mechanization|No exports - contribution of exports to total turnover is Nil|Markets served: 2 states in India; no international locations

currentContext.expansion: The routed annual-report text discloses no named expansion, capacity-addition, commissioning or debottlenecking project. The Company's footprint is described in BRSR Section A as a single plant and a single office, both national and none international, with markets served in 2 states and no international presence. The only forward capital language is generic dividend-policy wording that retained earnings may be used for capital expenditure for working capital, organic and/or inorganic growth and long-term investments; no project, quantum or timeline is attached to it. The MD&A notes that 79% of total non-current assets is represented by property, plant and equipment (including capital work-in-progress), but no expansion narrative accompanies it. Operationally, engines supplied during fiscal 2026 stood at 2,02,771 units against 1,68,820 units in the previous year, without any stated installed-capacity or utilisation figure.
currentContext.mdna: Medium-term outlook for the Indian tractor industry described as positive, supported by increasing farm mechanization, rising rural wages, continued labour shortages, and growing use of tractors in non-agricultural applications|Domestic volumes expected to normalize following a record FY26, in which the domestic tractor industry crossed the one-million-unit milestone for the first time at 11,60,300 units, a growth of 23% over the previous year's 9,39,700 units|Gradual mix shift towards higher horsepower tractors (40-60 HP), greater adoption of four-wheel-drive variants, and increasing penetration of precision farming technologies|Compact tractors below 30 HP gaining importance in horticulture, orchard farming and fragmented landholding regions, while the 31-50 HP category still accounts for the majority of demand|Government initiatives promoting mechanization - subsidy support, affordable credit availability, low GST rate, and expansion of custom hiring centres and rental / 'Tractor as a Service' models - expected to enhance accessibility for small and marginal farmers|Rising demand from eastern and central regions, plus diversification into horticulture and allied activities, expected to support sustained demand|Industry progressing towards technological upgradation and cleaner solutions, with preparedness for evolving emission norms and early investments in alternative fuel and electric tractor platforms|Structural headwinds flagged: fragmented landholdings, rising input costs, and climatic variability; demand also closely influenced by monsoon conditions, crop realizations and government interventions|Company-level cost narrative: material cost at 78.3% of net revenue from operations against the previous year's 78.9%, while other expenses rose to 5.6% of net operating revenue from 4.7%, reflecting normal inflation, higher CSR expense, hire & service charges, warranty, repair & maintenance and R&D expense

risks.risk: Total customer concentration - the entire output is sold to Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd., which is also the holding company
risks.note: BRSR Section A states 'The Company is in the business of manufacturing diesel engines and its entire sale to Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. ("M&M") for fitment into "Swaraj" tractors being manufactured by M&M', and M&M holds 52.11%. The MD&A adds: 'As a supplier to M&M, your Company would be directly affected by factors impacting tractor industry.' Any change in M&M's sourcing, in-housing of engines, or Swaraj-brand volumes flows straight through to the Company, and the pricing of virtually all its revenue is set inside a related-party arrangement (FY 2025-26 transaction value with M&M of Rs. 2026.67 crores, stated to be at arm's length).

risks.risk: Dependence on a monsoon- and policy-driven agricultural cycle
risks.note: Management explicitly flags 'the rain-dependent nature of our agriculture, Government policy on procurement, credit availability' as factors affecting it. Tractor demand is described as 'closely influenced by monsoon conditions, crop realizations, government interventions, and the pace of farm mechanization', and the industry outlook names 'climatic variability' as a structural challenge. Volumes are therefore outside management's control.

risks.risk: High-base risk after a record FY26 - industry volumes expected to normalize
risks.note: The domestic tractor industry crossed one million units for the first time in FY26 at 11,60,300 units, up 23%, and the Company's engine supply rose to 2,02,771 units from 1,68,820. Management itself states 'domestic volumes are expected to normalize following a record FY26', so the FY26 base embeds cyclical peak volumes that need not repeat.

risks.risk: Input-cost / commodity price exposure on a thin conversion margin
risks.note: Management lists 'commodity price trends' among the factors that would directly affect the Company, and the industry section names 'rising input costs' as a structural challenge. Material cost is 78.3% of net revenue from operations (previous year 78.9%), so a small unrecovered movement in input prices is material to profitability, particularly given a single-customer pricing structure.

risks.risk: Regulatory and emission-norm changes for tractors
risks.note: 'New regulations for tractors' is listed by management as a direct risk factor, and the industry is described as 'undergoing gradual technological and regulatory transitions with... preparedness for evolving emission norms'. Emission-norm transitions force engine redesign and re-certification cost onto the engine supplier.

risks.risk: Technology-transition risk to alternative fuel and electric tractor platforms
risks.note: The MD&A notes 'initial investments in alternative fuel and electric tractor platforms signal a long term shift towards sustainable mechanization'. The Company's business is 100% diesel engines and their components (NIC 29104), so a shift away from the diesel powertrain is an existential product risk rather than a mix risk.

BRSR Section A records one plant and one office, both national, with no international locations; markets served span 2 states; exports are Nil; and 100% of turnover comes from manufacturing of diesel engines and components. There is no product, site or geographic diversification to absorb a disruption at the Mohali works or in the domestic tractor cycle.

risks.risk: Ethical conduct, governance and compliance - flagged by the Company itself as a Risk in its BRSR materiality table
risks.note: The only BRSR material issue classified as a 'Risk' (rather than an Opportunity) is 'Ethical behaviour, Governance and Compliance', with the rationale that 'Any non-compliance could lead to litigation and may also impact the brand reputation'. Mitigation cited is a code of conduct for directors and employees plus a whistle-blower policy covering directors, employees, vendors, suppliers and other stakeholders.
